doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
This e-Tax Guide provides information on the determination of the date of
commencement of a business.
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 1 Aim > para 1
heading: 1 Aim
cite: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business, para 1

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
Generally, a business may be regarded as having commenced operation
when the business has established its profit-making structure and started its
first commercial activity.
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 2 At a glance > para 2.1
heading: 2 At a glance
cite: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business, para 2.1

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
In determining the date of commencement of business by a taxpayer, the
Comptroller of Income Tax (“CIT”) requires the following facts for
examination:
(i) description of the taxpayer’s main business and the activities carried on
by the business;
(ii) description of profit-making structure of the identified business;
(iii) whether the company has begun its day-to-day business operations; and
(iv) chronological list of key events leading up to the profit-making structure
being operationally ready and the time when the taxpayer starts its
ordinary business activities.
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 2 At a glance > para 2.2
heading: 2 At a glance
cite: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business, para 2.2

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
Once the date of commencement of business is ascertained, all expenses
incurred prior to this date are pre-commencement expenses and would not
qualify for tax deduction.
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 2 At a glance > para 2.3
heading: 2 At a glance
cite: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business, para 2.3

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
The deductibility of outgoings and expenses of a business is governed by
the provisions of sections 14 and 15 of the Income Tax Act 1947 (2020
Revised Edition) (“ITA”). Under section 14(1), only outgoings and expenses
that are wholly and exclusively incurred in the production of income are tax
deductible.
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 3 Background > para 3.1
heading: 3 Background
cite: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business, para 3.1

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
All outgoings and expenses incurred prior to the date on which a business
commences operation are not wholly and exclusively incurred in the
production of income. Hence, such expenses do not qualify for tax deduction.
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 3 Background > para 3.2
heading: 3 Background
cite: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business, para 3.2

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
In the Year of Assessment 2004, a concession for enterprise development
was introduced. Under this concession, a business will be treated as having
commenced its operations on the first day of the accounting year in which it
1
earns its first dollar of business receipt (i.e. deemed date of commencement
of business). As such, revenue expenses incurred in the aforesaid
accounting year, including those incurred prior to the day on which the
business earns its first dollar of receipt, will be deductible for tax purposes.
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 3 Background > para 3.3
heading: 3 Background
cite: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business, para 3.3

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
With effect from YA 2012, the concession for enterprise development was
enhanced to allow a deduction for revenue expenses incurred 1 year prior to
the deemed date of commencement of business.
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 3 Background > para 3.4
heading: 3 Background
cite: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business, para 3.4

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
The concession for enterprise development does not preclude a business
from substantiating that it has commenced operation earlier than the
accounting year in which it earns its first dollar of business receipt.
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 3 Background > para 3.5
heading: 3 Background
cite: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business, para 3.5

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
The ITA does not provide any definition on when a business is regarded as
having commenced its operation. The date of commencement of a business
depends on the facts of each case. Based on principles drawn from case
laws, it is only when the business has established its profit-making structure
and started its first commercial activity that it can be regarded as having
commenced operation.
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 4 Information to determine the date of commencement of business > para 4.1
heading: 4 Information to determine the date of commencement of business
cite: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business, para 4.1

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
What constitutes “a profit-making structure” will differ from business to
business. The type of activities a business primarily engages in will
determine its profit-making structure and the operational readiness of such
structure. For example, in a case of hotelier, the profit-making structure can
be said to be in place when the hotel licence is obtained. This is when the
hotel premises would have been fully constructed and the internal fittings
installed. It is upon obtaining this licence that the hotel can start its operation
and receive its first guest.
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 4 Information to determine the date of commencement of business > para 4.2
heading: 4 Information to determine the date of commencement of business

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
In determining the date of commencement of business by a taxpayer, the
CIT generally requires the following facts for examination:
(i) description of the taxpayer’s main business and the activities carried on
by the business;
(ii) description of profit-making structure of the identified business;
(iii) whether the company has begun its day-to-day business operations; and
(iv) chronological list of key events leading up to the profit-making structure
being operationally ready and the time when the taxpayer starts its
2
ordinary business activities.
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 4 Information to determine the date of commencement of business > para 4.3
heading: 4 Information to determine the date of commencement of business
cite: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business, para 4.3

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
In the course of evaluating the facts, the CIT will distinguish activities that are
merely preparatory or preliminary in nature from those conducted by the
business on a day-to-day basis. Preparatory or preliminary activities are
typically activities undertaken by the taxpayer before it is in a position to
derive income. Such activities may include signing a business contract,
obtaining a loan to build infrastructure for the business and
construction/building of the infrastructure.
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 4 Information to determine the date of commencement of business > para 4.4
heading: 4 Information to determine the date of commencement of business
cite: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business, para 4.4

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
Once the date of commencement of business is ascertained, all expenses
incurred prior to this date, being pre-commencement or pre- operating
expenses, would not qualify for tax deduction under section 14(1).

text:
Date of
Amendments made
amendment
1 29 July 2014 Paragraph 3.4 is inserted to highlight that the
concession for enterprise development has been
enhanced to allow a deduction for revenue expenses
incurred 1 year prior to the deemed date of
commencement of business.
2 23 Mar 2022 1. Footnote 1 has been updated to make reference to
the renumbered provision in the Income Tax Act
1947 (2020 Revised Edition)
2. The examples in the Annex have been updated to
more recent dates.
4
Annex – Illustrations of date of commencement of business
(I) Wholesale and Retail
A trader in the wholesale and retail industries is considered to have
commenced its business when it opens its door to the public.
Example (Supermarket)
Date Event
1.1.2020 Incorporation of company
1.2.2020 Signed tenancy agreement for business premises,
purchased office equipment, recruited staff, placed orders
for products to be sol
1.4.2020 Retail stock arrived and arranged on shelves
9.4.2020 Supermarket opened its door to the public
1.6.2020 Official opening ceremony
The supermarket is considered to have commenced business when it
opened its door and offered its goods for sale to the public. Thus, its date
of commencement would be 9.4.2020. The opening ceremony is merely
ceremonial and does not alter the actual date of commencement.
5
(II) Hoteliers
Under the Hotels Act, a hotel operator is required to register the premises
with the Hotels Licensing Board (“HLB”) before it can operate as a hotel.
Typically, when an application to HLB is made, the hotel premises should
be fully constructed and the internal fittings installed. Otherwise, it will not
be able to meet the conditions for registration as a hotel. The hotel is only
allowed to receive its first guest upon obtaining the certificate of registration.
CIT, therefore, considers a hotel to have commenced its business on the
date of certificate of registration.
Example
Date Event
6.1.2019 Purchased land to construct hotel premises
1.3.2019 Began construction of hotel premises
2.6.2020 Conducted training for staff
1.7.2020 Applied for hotel registration certificate
2.8.2020 Obtained certificate of hotel registration
The activities carried out by the hotelier prior to 2.8.2020 were merely
preparatory in nature. The business would be regarded as having
commenced on 2.8.2020, which is the date it obtained its certificate of
hotel registration. This is the earliest date it could operate as a hotelier
and receive its first guest.
6
(III) Manufacturing
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 6 Updates and amendments > para 6
heading: 6 Updates and amendments
cite: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business, para 6

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
A manufacturer is considered to have commenced business when its profit-
making structure capable of commercial production has been put in place.
Generally, the date on which the manufacturer commenced commercial
production is taken as the date of commencement of business.
Example (Manufacturer of electronic components)
Date Event
2.1.2019 Incorporation of company
1.12.2019 Completed construction of manufacturing plant
5.12.2019 Obtained relevant licences to manufacture
components
8.12.2019 Recruited staff
15.12.2019 Installed plant and machinery
20.12.2019 Sent engineers and technical specialist for training
15.1.2020 Purchased raw materials
30.1.2020 Tested product during trial run before commercial
production
15.2.2020 Commenced commercial production
25.2.2020 Made first sale
The manufacturer is considered to have commenced business when it
started its first commercial production on 15.2.2020. Licences and other
expenses incurred prior to 15.2.2020 are pre-commencement expenses.
These expenses relate to preliminary work done in preparation for the
commencement of business and hence not tax deductible.
7
(IV) Property Developer
A newly incorporated property development company which develops
properties for sale is regarded as having commenced business on the date
it acquires a land/building for development for sale. All expenses incurred
prior to the date of acquisition of the land/building are pre-commencement
expenses and therefore do not qualify for tax deduction. Expenses, such as
cost of land, construction cost, financing cost and property tax incurred in
the course of the property development would be capitalised as part of the
development costs. These capitalised costs would qualify for tax deduction
as cost of sale when the Temporary Occupation Permit is issued.
8
(V) Proprietary Club
The main business of a proprietary club involves the sale of club
memberships and the operation of the club. The main source of income for
such business is usually from the sale of its club memberships. Thus, the
proprietary club is generally regarded as having commenced business on
the date it first launches its membership drive. All revenue expenses
incurred on or after the date of the launch are tax deductible.
Example
Date Event
16.10.2018 Purchased land to build clubhouse
12.11.2018 Conducted recruitment and staff training exercises
15.12.2018 Launched its membership drive through
advertisements and promotional campaigns
3.1.2019 Commenced construction of clubhouse
3.2.2019 Received first club membership fees from members
13.3.2020 Completed the construction of clubhouse
1.4.2020 Clubhouse facilities were opened to members
The proprietary club would be regarded as having commenced its
path: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business > 6 Updates and amendments > para 6
heading: 6 Updates and amendments
cite: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business, para 6

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Date of Commencement of Business
text:
business on 15.12.2018 when it first launched its club membership drive.
It is through its advertisement and marketing efforts that the business was
able to derive its earnings. This is notwithstanding that the club only
received its first membership fees on 3.2.2019 and the clubhouse facilities
were opened on 1.4.2020.
All activities carried out prior to 15.12.2018 were preparatory in nature.
Thus, expenses incurred prior to 15.12.2018 are pre- commencement
expenses and do not qualify for tax deduction.
9
(VI) Professional Services
A business which provides professional services such as fund management
services is considered to have commenced operation when the necessary set-up
for the activities that enables it to conduct its day-to-day operation is in place.
Generally, this is when the business is ready to market its services and conclude
contracts with its potential clients.
Example (Fund management services)
Date Event
10.1.2018 Incorporation of the company
15.11.2018 Establishment of office
30.11.2018 Recruited fund managers and other office staff
15.3.2019 Commenced to market its fund management
products/services
4.1.2020 Commenced to derive income
The business of fund management commenced on 15.3.2019 when the
company was able to market its products and services. This is
notwithstanding that the company only started to derive its income on
4.1.2020.
In the context of the fund management business, the marketing activities
are part of the company’s regular business activities and are integral to its
day-to-day operations. The necessary set-up was in place on 15.3.2019
for the marketing activities to be conducted. Expenses, to establish an
office and recruit the fund managers and other office staff, incurred prior
to 15.3.2019 were preparatory in nature. These are pre-commencement
expenses and are not tax deductible.
10

text: This e-Tax Guide provides details on the carry-back relief system.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 1 Aim > para 1.1
heading: 1 Aim
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 1.1

text:
The e-Tax Guide is relevant to you if you have unabsorbed capital
allowances (“CA”) or unabsorbed trade losses from your trade,
business, profession or vocation for the current year.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 1 Aim > para 1.2
heading: 1 Aim
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 1.2

text:
The carry-back relief under section 37D of the Income Tax Act (“ITA”) is
available to all persons carrying on a business, including sole-
proprietorships and partnerships. The relief will be given only if a claim
is made for it.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 2 At a glance > para 2.1
heading: 2 At a glance
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 2.1

text:
Under the system, a person may carry back its current year qualifying
deductions (“QD”) and deduct them against its assessable income of the
immediate preceding YA. For YAs 2020 and 2021, a person may elect
to carry back QD and deduct them against its assessable income for up
to three YAs immediately preceding the relevant YA of loss (i.e. YA 2017,
YA 2018 and YA 2019 where the YA of loss is YA 2020, and YA 2018,
YA 2019 and YA 2020 where the YA of loss is YA 2021) (referred to as
“enhanced carry-back relief” in this e-Tax Guide). To ease businesses’
cash flow, a person may also elect for carry-back relief or enhanced
carry-back relief based on an estimate of the QD for YAs 2020 and 2021.
Please refer to the e-Tax Guide on “Enhanced Carry-back Relief
System” for more details on the enhanced carry-back relief for YAs 2020
and 2021.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 2 At a glance > para 2.2
heading: 2 At a glance
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 2.2

text:
The maximum amount of QD that can be carried back is capped at
$100,000.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 2 At a glance > para 2.3
heading: 2 At a glance
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 2.3

text:
The QD will be deducted in the following order:
(i) current year’s unabsorbed CA, if any,
(ii) current year’s trade losses, if any.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 2 At a glance > para 2.4
heading: 2 At a glance
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 2.4

text:
The carry-back of unabsorbed CA is subject to the “same business” test.
A company will have to satisfy the shareholding test as well.
A company can elect to carry back its QD after transferring its loss
items under the group relief system, if applicable.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 2 At a glance > para 2.5
heading: 2 At a glance
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 2.5

text:
Assessable income
Assessable income of a company refers to its income from all sources
after deducting CA, trade losses, approved donations (including those
transferred from related companies under the group relief system) and
other relevant deductions like incremental research and development
expenses or investment allowances.
Assessable income of an individual refers to the individual’s income from
all sources after deducting CA, losses, and approved donations.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 3 Glossary > para 3.1
heading: 3 Glossary
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 3.1

text:
Immediate Preceding YA
The immediate preceding YA refers to the YA immediately before the YA
in which the person has trade losses or capital allowances available for
carry back. For example, if the person incurred trade losses or was
granted capital allowances in YA 2020, the immediate preceding YA
would be YA 2019.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 3 Glossary > para 3.2
heading: 3 Glossary
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 3.2

text:
Loss items
For group relief purposes, loss items refer to the unabsorbed CA, trade
losses and donations for the current year that can be transferred by a
company (“transferor company”) to another company of the group
(“claimant company”).
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 3 Glossary > para 3.3
heading: 3 Glossary
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 3.3

text:
Person
A person in this e-Tax Guide refers to:
a. a company;
b. an individual, being the sole-proprietor or partner of a partnership
[including a limited liability partnership (“LLP”) and a limited
partnership (“LP”)];
c. a body of persons, such as clubs and associations; and
d. a trustee of a trust or an executor of an estate.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 3 Glossary > para 3.4
heading: 3 Glossary
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 3.4

text:
Qualifying deductions (QD)
For carry-back relief purposes, QD are the unabsorbed CA and
unabsorbed trade losses for the current year.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 3 Glossary > para 3.5
heading: 3 Glossary
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 3.5

text:
Relevant deductions
A limited partner’s share of CA and trade losses from a limited liability
partnership (“LLP”) or limited partnership (“LP”) allowed against the
partner’s income from other sources.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 3 Glossary > para 3.6
heading: 3 Glossary
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 3.6

text:
Same business test
This test determines if a person continues to carry on the same trade,
business or profession for which capital allowances are granted when
carrying forward or back the unabsorbed capital allowances. The test is
satisfied if the same trade, business or profession is being continued at
the point when the unabsorbed capital allowances are utilised.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 3 Glossary > para 3.7
heading: 3 Glossary
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 3.7

text:
Shareholding test
This test computes the percentage of the shareholdings of a company
(or its ultimate parent company) that is held by the same persons as at
the relevant dates. If the percentage is 50% or more, there is no
substantial change in the shareholders and the company is said to have
satisfied the shareholding test.
Relevant dates for unabsorbed CA:
First day of the YA in which the capital allowances were granted and the
last day of the immediate preceding YA in which the capital allowances
are to be deducted.
Relevant dates for unabsorbed trade losses:
First day of the year in which the trade losses were incurred and last day
of the immediate preceding YA in which the trade losses are to be
deducted.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 3 Glossary > para 3.8
heading: 3 Glossary
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 3.8

text:
Unabsorbed capital allowances (CA)
The capital allowances claimed by a person (under section 16, 17, 18B,
18C, 19, 19A, 19B, 19C, 19D or 20 of the ITA) for a YA that exceed the
person’s aggregate taxable income for that YA.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 3 Glossary > para 3.9
heading: 3 Glossary
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 3.9

text:
Unabsorbed trade losses
The trade losses incurred by a person for a YA that exceed the person’s
income from all sources for that YA.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 3 Glossary > para 3.10
heading: 3 Glossary
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 3.10

text:
Unabsorbed donations
The approved donations made by a person in a YA that exceeds its
statutory income for that YA. Approved donations are donations
qualifying for tax deduction and made to recipients under sections 37(3)
(b), (c), (d), (e) or (f) of the ITA.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 3 Glossary > para 3.11
heading: 3 Glossary
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 3.11

text:
Before YA 2006, a person may carry forward its unabsorbed CA and
trade losses to future YAs if it satisfies certain conditions under the ITA.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 4 Background > para 4.1
heading: 4 Background
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 4.1

text:
To help small businesses cope with cash-flow problems, especially in a
cyclical downturn, a one year carry-back of QD was introduced from the
YA 2006.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 4 Background > para 4.2
heading: 4 Background
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 4.2

text:
Subject to conditions, the carry-back relief is available to you as a person
(defined in paragraph 3.4 above) who carries on a trade, business,
profession or vocation.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 5 Carry-back relief system > para 5.1
heading: 5 Carry-back relief system
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 5.1

text:
You may carry back the QD to the immediate preceding YA to be
deducted from your assessable income of the immediate preceding YA
in the order set out in paragraphs 6.8 and 6.9.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 5 Carry-back relief system > para 5.2
heading: 5 Carry-back relief system
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 5.2

text:
Your claim for carry-back relief is subject to the following general
conditions:
(a) Same business test
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief > para 6.1
heading: 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 6.1

text:
To qualify for carry-back relief, you must satisfy the same business test.
This means that you will not be able to carry back the unabsorbed CA
granted for the first basis period that you commenced a trade, business
or profession. However, you can carry back the trade loss incurred for
that period as the same business test does not apply to trade losses.
To illustrate:
During the basis period for YA 2018 that you commenced a business,
you incurred a trade loss of $50,000 and had unabsorbed CA of $20,000.
You could carry back the trade loss of $50,000 (but not the unabsorbed
CA of $20,000) to be deducted against your assessable income for YA
2017.
(b) Shareholding test
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief > para 6.2
heading: 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 6.2

text:
If you are a company, in addition to the same business test, you have to
satisfy the shareholding test in order to carry back your QD.
To illustrate:
For YA 2018, your accounting period is 1 Jan 2017 to 31 Dec 2017. You
can carry back your QD for YA 2018 to YA 2017 if your shareholders as
at the following dates are substantially the same:
Dates for comparison
Unabsorbed CA
1 Jan 2018 1 day of the YA in which the CA arose; &
&
Carry-back of
31 Dec Last day of the YA in which the CA is utilised
2017
1 Jan 2017 1 day of the year in which the loss was
Trade loss
& incurred; &
31 Dec Last day of the YA in which the loss is utilised
2017
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief > para 6.3
heading: 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 6.3

text:
The Comptroller of Income Tax (“CIT”) may waive the shareholding test
if it is satisfied that the substantial change in the shareholders is not for
the purpose of deriving any tax benefit or obtaining any tax advantage.
If the CIT grants the waiver, you can only deduct the QD against the
income from the same trade or business for which the CA was granted
or to which the trade loss relates.
(c) Amount of Qualifying deductions to be carried back
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief > para 6.4
heading: 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 6.4

text:
The amount of QD that you can carry back is restricted to the lowest of:
(i) your actual amount of the QD;
(ii) your assessable income of the immediate preceding YA; and
(iii) $100,000.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief > para 6.5
heading: 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 6.5

text:
The excess that is not carried back can be carried forward for deduction
against your future taxable income if you satisfy the same business test
(and shareholding test if you are a company).
To illustrate:
Your assessable income for YA 2017 = $60,000
Your QD for YA 2018 = $72,000
Amount of QD you can carry back to YA 2017 = $60,000
Excess that you can carry forward for deduction = $12,000
against future taxable income
Annex A shows how to determine the amount of QD to be carried back.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief > para 6.6
heading: 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 6.6

text:
If your functional currency is not S$, the exchange rate to use for the
purpose of computing the cap of $100,000 is based on the exchange
rate of the year in which the loss arose.
To illustrate:

The exchange rate is 1.3833 for YA 2017 and 1.3749 for YA 2018.
You incurred a trade loss of US$150,000 for the YA 2018.
The amount of trade loss that you can carry back for deduction against

path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief > para 6.7
heading: 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 6.7

text:
The QD carried back will be deducted from your assessable income of
the immediate preceding YA in the following order:
(a) current year unabsorbed CA, if any; and then
(b) current year trade loss, if any.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief > para 6.8
heading: 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 6.8

text:
If you have other income in addition to trade income, the unabsorbed CA
and trade losses will be deducted against the other sources of income in
the order as follows:
1 : Income from same trade
2 : Income from other trade (proportionately if there is more than
one other trade, business, profession or vocation)
3rd : Income from all other sources (proportionately if there is more
than one other sources)
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief > para 6.9
heading: 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 6.9

text:
Where your QD exceed $100,000, and they arose from more than one
trade, business, profession or vocation, the amount you can carry back
for each of the trade, business, profession or vocation is also determined
on a proportionate basis.
Annex B provides examples on the order of deducting the QD carried
back where there is more than:
(i) one trade source; and
(ii) one source of other income.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief > para 6.10
heading: 6 General Conditions Governing the Carry-Back Relief
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 6.10

text: (a) Where income is taxed at concessionary rate
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 7 Carry- back relief under specific scenarios > para 7
heading: 7 Carry- back relief under specific scenarios
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 7

text:
If you are a company or a body of persons with income chargeable to
tax at the normal corporate tax rate, but your QD relate to income
chargeable to tax at concessionary tax rate, the adjustment provided
under section 37A of the ITA, (“adjustment factor”) has be applied for
deduction across income chargeable under different tax rates.
path: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System > 7 Carry- back relief under specific scenarios > para 7.1
heading: 7 Carry- back relief under specific scenarios
cite: e-Tax Guide: Carry-back Relief System, para 7.1

text:
In addition, the amount of QD (up to $100,000) is determined based on
the following formula:
A + B
where A = any amount deducted against assessable income subject
to tax at the normal corporate tax rate (currently 17%);
B = any amount deducted against assessable income subject
to tax at any concessionary rate of tax divided by the
adjustment factor for that concessionary rate of tax;
and

text:
If you are a limited partner of an LLP or a LP, your relevant deductions,
together with all of your relevant deductions allowed in all past YAs, must
not exceed your contributed capital as at the end of the basis period
relating to that YA. This restriction is known as the “relevant deduction
restriction”. Any excess of the relevant deductions over your contributed
capital may then (subject to conditions) be carried forward to be
deducted against your future share of income from the same LLP or LP.

back relief. Your capital contribution as at the end of the basis period
relating to the YA that the QD arise will be used for the relevant deduction
restriction. This is because your QD to be carried back relate to that YA
and not the immediate preceding YA.

text:
You will not be able to carry back your QD if the QD arise from certain
trade or activity carried on. They are:
(a) Qualifying deductions of a trade where the income is wholly
exempt from tax
If you carry on such a trade (e.g. pioneer trade), you are not
allowed to carry back the QD relating to that trade for deduction
against other exempt or non-exempt income.
(b) Qualifying deductions of specific activity or trade
If you carry on specific types of activity or trade where there are
rules restricting the deduction of the QD only against such trade
or activity, or restricting the carry forward of the QD, you are to
apply the same restriction in the carry back of the QD. The QD
from such trade or activities are not allowed to be deducted
against your other sources of income.
These activities or trades include:
(i) finance leasing where the income is taxable under section
10C of the ITA; and
(ii) the business of hiring out motor cars where the income is
taxable under section 10F of the ITA.
(c) Qualifying deductions of a Section 10D company
If you carry on a business of the making of investments, you are
not allowed to carry forward your QD arising from that business.
As the QD are disregarded, the carry- back relief does not apply.
(d) Loss of eligible investors in approved start-up companies
under the Enterprise Investment Incentive Scheme (EII)
Currently, an eligible investor holding qualifying shares in
approved start-up under the Enterprise Investment Incentive
scheme (EII) may incur a capital loss upon:
(i) the sale of its qualifying shares; or
(ii) the liquidation of the approved start-up companies.
As the loss is capital in nature, it does not qualify for carry- back
relief.

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
This e-Tax Guide explains the tax deduction granted under section 14N of
the Income Tax Act 1947 (“ITA”) for capital expenses incurred by taxpayers
for the renovation or refurbishment works done to their business premises
(“R&R expenditure”).
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 1 Aim > para 1.1
heading: 1 Aim
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 1.1

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
This e-Tax Guide is relevant to a taxpayer carrying on a trade, business or
profession and has incurred expenditure on any renovation or refurbishment
works for that trade, business or profession.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 1 Aim > para 1.2
heading: 1 Aim
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 1.2

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
Certain qualifying capital expenses, up to an expenditure cap, incurred on or
after 16 Feb 2008 for the renovation or refurbishment works done to the
business premises can be claimed as tax deductions against the income
derived from that business.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 2 At a glance > para 2.1
heading: 2 At a glance
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 2.1

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
The deduction is given over a period of three consecutive years on a straight-
line basis, starting from the year of assessment (“YA”) for which those
expenses were incurred.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 2 At a glance > para 2.2
heading: 2 At a glance
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 2.2

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
For qualifying R&R expenditure incurred in the basis period for YAs 2021,
2022, 2024 and from 2025 onwards (i.e. financial years 2020, 2021, 2023
and from 2024 onwards respectively), a taxpayer has the option to claim the
deduction in one year instead of over three years, as announced in Budget
2020, 2021, 2023 and 2024.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 2 At a glance > para 2.3
heading: 2 At a glance
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 2.3

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
S14N deductions can be claimed on qualifying R&R expenditure up to an
expenditure cap of $300,000 for every three-year period (“relevant three-year
period”), starting from the YA in which the business first incurred R&R
expenditure and made a claim.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 2 At a glance > para 2.4
heading: 2 At a glance
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 2.4

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
As announced in Budget 2024, the relevant three-year period will be fixed for
all taxpayers from YA 2025 (i.e. financial year 2024) onwards, with the first
fixed three-year period being from YA 2025 to YA 2027.

heading: 2 At a glance

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
Businesses often need to renovate or refurbish their business premises to
remain competitive and to attract customers. Such R&R expenditure are
generally capital expenses unless they relate to repairs or replacement works
on the premises with no improvement element. Such capital expenses are
not permissible deductions under the ITA unless specific provisions are
made to allow them.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 3 Background > para 3.1
heading: 3 Background
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 3.1

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
To help businesses, especially small and medium enterprises, reduce
business costs, section 14N was introduced into the ITA to allow a tax
deduction for qualifying R&R expenditure incurred by businesses. The
deduction, henceforth referred to in this e-Tax Guide as “S14N deduction”, is
applicable to the R&R expenditure incurred on or after 16 Feb 2008.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 3 Background > para 3.2
heading: 3 Background
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 3.2

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
S14N deduction is given over a period of three consecutive years, on a
straight-line basis, starting from the YA for which the qualifying R&R
expenditure were incurred. The claim for S14N deduction cannot be deferred.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 4 S14N Deduction > para 4.1
heading: 4 S14N Deduction
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 4.1

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
As announced in Budget 2020, 2021 and 2023, a taxpayer will be given the
option to claim qualifying R&R expenditure incurred in the basis period for
YA 2021 (i.e. financial year 2020), YA 2022 (i.e. financial year 2021) and YA
2024 (i.e. financial year 2023) in one year instead of over three years. From
YA 2025 onwards, the option to claim qualifying R&R expenditure in one year
instead of over three years will be permanently available to businesses, as
announced in Budget 2024. The option, once elected in the YA, is irrevocable.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 4 S14N Deduction > para 4.2
heading: 4 S14N Deduction
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 4.2

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
S14N deduction is given as long as the trade, business or profession for
which the R&R expenditure is incurred, is carried on during the basis period.
If no income is derived from the trade, business or profession in any YA and
that trade, business or profession ceases permanently during the basis
period for that YA, no S14N deduction is to be given in that YA.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 4 S14N Deduction > para 4.3
heading: 4 S14N Deduction
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 4.3

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
S14N deduction can be claimed on qualifying R&R expenditure up to an
expenditure cap of $300,000 for every three-year period (“relevant three-
year period”), starting from the YA in which the business first incurred R&R
expenditure and claimed deductions under S14N. Please refer to question 2
1 Section 15(1)(c) and 15(1)(d) of the ITA.
2 Prior to YA 2013, the expenditure cap was $150,000 for every relevant three-year period. This cap
3
was increased to $300,000 from YA 2013 onwards.
of the Annex for an illustration of how the relevant three-year period is
identified.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 5 Expenditure cap > para 5.1
heading: 5 Expenditure cap
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 5.1

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
In the case of partnerships, the expenditure cap of $300,000 is applied at the
partnership level. For a sole proprietor, the same expenditure cap is
applicable regardless of the number of trades being carried on.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 5 Expenditure cap > para 5.2
heading: 5 Expenditure cap
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 5.2

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
As announced in Budget 2024, to ease businesses’ compliance burden, the
relevant three-year period for claiming R&R expenditure will be fixed for all
businesses, with the first fixed three-year period being from YA 2025 to YA
2027 (see table below). This will replace the regime where the relevant three-
year period depends on when the business first incurred R&R expenditure
and made a claim under Section 14N.
Fixed Three-Year Periods Expenditure Cap
YA 2025 to YA 2027 $300,000
YA 2028 to YA 2030 $300,000
YA 2031 to YA 2033 $300,000
YA 2034 to YA 2036; and so on $300,000
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 5 Expenditure cap > para 5.3
heading: 5 Expenditure cap
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 5.3

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
As a transitional measure, a taxpayer whose current relevant three-year
period does not coincide with the first fixed three-year period (i.e. YA 2025
to YA 2027) will be allowed a refreshed expenditure cap of $300,000 for the
period from YA 2025 to YA 2027. Please refer to question 3 of the Annex for
illustrations of how the relevant three-year period is determined from YA
2025.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 5 Expenditure cap > para 5.4
heading: 5 Expenditure cap
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 5.4

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
Taxpayers who do not carry on a trade or business throughout the entire
fixed three-year period will also be allowed the full expenditure cap of
$300,000 for each fixed three-year period. There will be no proration of the
expenditure cap. For example, a newly incorporated company which
commences business in YA 2026 will be allowed an expenditure cap of
$300,000 for YA 2026 and YA 2027.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 5 Expenditure cap > para 5.5
heading: 5 Expenditure cap
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 5.5

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
If the renovation or refurbishment works qualify as repairs or replacements
with no improvement element, tax deduction can be claimed under section
14(1)(c) of the ITA. Similarly, if the R&R expenditure qualifies as expenses
incurred on purchase of plant or machinery under section 19 or section 19A
of the ITA, capital allowances can be claimed under those sections. In these
scenarios, S14N deduction cannot be claimed on the same R&R expenditure
incurred.
4
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 6 No double deduction > para 6.1
heading: 6 No double deduction
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 6.1

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
S14N deduction is allowed against the income from the trade, business or
profession for which the R&R expenditure is incurred, after all other
deductions under Part 5 (Deductions against income) of the ITA have been
allowed.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 7 Group relief and loss carry-back relief > para 7.1
heading: 7 Group relief and loss carry-back relief
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 7.1

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
Any unabsorbed S14N deduction due to insufficient trade income forms part
of the trade losses for which the normal tax treatment for trade losses applies.
This means that such unabsorbed S14N deduction can be carried forward
for offset against income in subsequent YAs, subject to the provisions of
section 37 of the ITA. It can also qualify for group relief under section 37B
of the ITA and loss carry-back relief under section 37D of the ITA, subject to
the provisions of those sections.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 7 Group relief and loss carry-back relief > para 7.2
heading: 7 Group relief and loss carry-back relief
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 7.2

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
All R&R expenditure, other than those relating to structural changes made to
business premises and the costs described in paragraph 8.3, will qualify for
S14N deduction, up to the expenditure cap.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 8 Qualifying R&R expenditure > para 8.1
heading: 8 Qualifying R&R expenditure
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 8.1

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
Under the Building Control Act, if structural changes are made to a building,
an approval from the Commissioner of Building Control is required. As long
as prior approval from the Commissioner of Building Control is not required
for the renovation or refurbishment works carried out in the business
premises, the R&R expenditure will be considered as qualifying R&R
expenditure for S14N deduction.
path: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works > 8 Qualifying R&R expenditure > para 8.2
heading: 8 Qualifying R&R expenditure
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 8.2

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
Claim for S14N deduction on the following expenditure is not allowable:
(a) any designer services or professional services, except designer
services or professional services which do not affect the structure of
the business premises from YA 2025;
(b) any antique;
(c) any type of fine art including painting, drawing, print, calligraphy,
mosaic, sculpture, pottery or art installation; or
(d) any works carried out to a place of residence provided to or to be
provided to employees.

text:
Taxpayers who wish to opt for the one-year write-off for S14N deduction in
respect of R&R expenditure incurred should indicate the election in the tax
computation submitted for the relevant YA. For taxpayers who are not
required to submit the tax computation (e.g. due to filing of Form C-S/ Form
C-S (Lite)/ Form B 2-line/ 4-line statement), the amount of allowable
expenses claimed, as declared in the tax return, would be the amount after
taking into account the one-year write-off for S14N deduction.

heading: 9 Administrative procedures
cite: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works, para 9.1

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
Taxpayers should maintain sufficient documents to substantiate their claims.
However, they do not need to submit these documents together with their tax
returns. They are only required to submit the supporting documents when
requested to do so as part of IRAS’ audit or verification process. Some
examples of supporting documents that should be retained are:
(a) An itemised list (including the related costs incurred) of the renovation
or refurbishment works done to the business premises with addresses
of the premises.

(b) Confirmation that the renovation or refurbishment works in the
itemised list do not require the approval of the Commissioner of
Building Control; and
(c) Invoices and payment details of the relevant expenditure.

doc_title: e-Tax Guide: Renovation or Refurbishment Works
text:
1. When can I claim S14N deduction?
You should claim S14N deduction on the qualifying R&R expenditure at the
time of lodgement of your tax return for the YA for which the R&R expenditure
is first incurred. Any qualifying R&R expenditure, which is not claimed in the
YA for which it is first incurred, do not qualify for deduction in subsequent
YAs. Any R&R expenditure which is incurred before you commence your
business is deemed to be incurred on the first day of the commencement of
your business. In such a case, you should claim the S14N deduction in the
YA which relates to the basis period in which you commence your business.

expenditure cap of $300,000 identified prior to YA 2025?

on its business premises during the period from 1 Mar 2018 to 31 Dec 2023

5. Can I claim a deduction under section 14(1)(c) on the costs I incur on
replacing a renovation item that was previously granted S14N
deduction?
Yes, provided the conditions under section 14(1)(c) are satisfied and the
deduction is not denied under section 15. Consequently, if you claim a
deduction under section 14(1)(c), you are not allowed S14N deduction on the
same replacement costs incurred by you.
6. Can the R&R expenditure incurred on premises that I use for both
business and other personal purposes (e.g. home offices) qualify for
S14N deduction?
For premises that are used for both business and other personal purposes,
only R&R expenditure which are specifically identifiable to the area that is
used for business purposes can qualify for S14N deduction. If you cannot
specifically identify the R&R expenditure to the area used for business
purposes, you are not allowed to claim S14N deduction, as no apportionment
of the R&R expenditure is allowable for tax purposes.
16
7. What are the tax consequences if I was required to seek the approval of
the Commissioner of Building Control for my renovation or
refurbishment works (as it involved structural changes) but failed to do
so, and I had claimed a S14N deduction on my R&R expenditure?
You should ensure that your R&R expenditure is qualifying expenditure
before making any S14N deduction claim.
If S14N deduction was erroneously allowed to you under such circumstance,
an amount equal to the total deductions that were erroneously allowed
previously is deemed as your taxable income for the YA in which the
Comptroller discovers the incorrect claim.
Where there is any form of fraud or wilful default committed by a taxpayer in
connection with its claim for R&R expenditure under section S14N, the
Comptroller can raise additional assessments on the taxpayer at any time as
provided under section 74(2) of the ITA. Additional penalties are applicable
under the ITA.

8. Is S14N deduction applicable to a business of making investments
which is subject to the provisions of section 10D of the ITA?
Yes. The business may claim S14N deduction on qualifying R&R expenditure
incurred on renovation or refurbishment works done to the properties which
are rented out by the business as part of its business of making investments.
